title: State ex rel. Office of the State Engineer v. Intrepid Potash, Inc.
description: Whether the district court and Court of Appeals erred in concluding Intrepid abandoned all but 150 acre-feet per year (afy) of its Pecos River water rights.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs (Respondents) argued that Intrepid Potash abandoned its water rights due to prolonged non-use and water speculation, which is contrary to the principle of beneficial use.
defendant_argument: The defendants (Petitioners) argued that the lower courts misapplied the abandonment test, confusing it with forfeiture, and that their actions demonstrated an intent not to abandon their water rights.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision, concluding that Intrepid Potash abandoned all but 150 acre-feet per year of its Pecos River water rights and that water speculation is contrary to beneficial use.

title: State v. Perea
description: Whether information provided by a confidential informant (CI) in a search warrant application satisfies the probable cause requirement under Article II, Section 10 of the New Mexico Constitution, with the plaintiff arguing it does and the defendant arguing it does not.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the affidavit established the CI had personal knowledge from first-hand observations of methamphetamine in the Petitioner's home, consistent with trafficking, which constitutes an adequate basis of knowledge for probable cause.
defendant_argument: The Petitioner argued the affidavit failed to demonstrate the CI's basis of knowledge with sufficient detail regarding the amount, packaging, or observed sales of methamphetamine, and that the warrant was overbroad.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Appeals' reversal of the district court's grant of the motion to suppress, thereby upholding the search warrant.

title: Bolen v. New Mexico Racing Commission
description: Whether judicial immunity is a defense available to a public body sued under the CRA, with the plaintiff arguing it is not and the defendant arguing it is.
plaintiff_argument: Bolen argued that judicial immunity is a doctrine that protects individuals, not governmental entities, and therefore a public body cannot rely on it as a defense to a CRA claim.
defendant_argument: NMRC argued that the CRA's plain language establishes that judicial immunity is an available defense for a public body.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed that judicial immunity is available to public bodies under the CRA but reversed the Court of Appeals' finding that NMRC was immune, remanding the case for further factual inquiry.

title: Stewart v. Ramczyk
description: Whether Senate President Pro Tempore Mimi Stewart is entitled to legislative immunity under the New Mexico Constitution's Speech or Debate Clause for reassigning Senator Jacob Candelaria's office and Senate floor seat, and whether a court can examine her motives to determine this immunity.
plaintiff_argument: Stewart argued that her actions of reassigning Candelaria's office and seat were legitimate legislative activities, making her entitled to legislative immunity and her motives irrelevant.
defendant_argument: Candelaria argued that Stewart's actions were unlawful retaliation, not legitimate legislative activities, and that the court should examine her motives, interpreting the New Mexico Speech or Debate Clause more narrowly.
decision_outcome: The court granted the writ of superintending control, holding that Stewart's motive is irrelevant and that she is entitled to legislative immunity, remanding the case to dismiss Candelaria's complaint.

title: State v. Maestas
description: Whether a contempt fine ordered payable to a third party is permitted under statute and the New Mexico Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The State argues that contempt fines payable to a third party are permitted and constitutional, as fines are not fees and are not collected by the judicial department, thus not subject to constitutional limitations on fees.
defendant_argument: Maestas argues that contempt fines must be paid directly to the court or state treasury, as fines are equivalent to fees under the constitution, and directing them to a third party is unconstitutional and could lead to judicial abuse.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the contempt fine ordered payable to a third party (the New Mexico State Bar Foundation) is permitted under the judiciary's inherent contempt power and is constitutional.

title: Amdor v. Grisham
description: Whether the Governor's emergency orders declaring gun violence and drug abuse as public health emergencies exceed the scope of the Public Health Emergency Response Act (PHERA), the proper scope of the police power, and violate separation-of-powers principles.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioners argued that the emergency orders exceeded the Governor's authority under PHERA, were an improper exercise of police power, and violated separation-of-powers principles because gun violence and drug abuse are not true public health emergencies under PHERA, and the orders encroached on legislative functions.
defendant_argument: The respondents argued that the emergency orders were within the Governor's authority under PHERA, were a proper exercise of police power, and did not violate separation-of-powers principles, as PHERA provides broad authority to respond to public health emergencies, and the orders were temporary measures.
decision_outcome: The court denied most of the petition, ruling that the emergency orders regarding gun violence and drug abuse did not violate the PHERA or separation-of-powers doctrine, but granted the petition to strike down the suspension of the Juvenile Detention Alternatives Initiative (JDAI) program as exceeding police power.

title: Johnson v. Board of Education
description: Whether a public school is a public accommodation under the New Mexico Human Rights Act (NMHRA), with the plaintiff arguing that it is, thereby subjecting schools to anti-discrimination suits, and the defendants arguing that it is not.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argues that public schools are public accommodations under the NMHRA, making them subject to anti-discrimination provisions, and that APS's educational services are open to all students, thus offering services to the public.
defendant_argument: The defendants argue that public schools are not public accommodations under the NMHRA, asserting that schools are traditional and historic institutions that existed before the Act and that a public accommodation must be a commercial business.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision, holding that a public school is a public accommodation under the NMHRA, and overruled a prior precedent that held public universities were not public accommodations in their academic programs.

title: State v. Vasquez
description: Whether a district court has the authority to independently initiate suppression hearings for warrantless searches, or if it must wait for a party to raise the issue.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the district court lacked standing and jurisdiction to sua sponte raise suppression issues, violated the separation of powers, and demonstrated bias by doing so.
defendant_argument: The defendant implicitly supported the district court's inherent authority to raise suppression issues sua sponte to protect fundamental rights against unreasonable searches and seizures.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the district court's inherent authority and jurisdiction to sua sponte raise suppression issues for warrantless searches, finding that such actions do not violate separation of powers or inherently demonstrate bias.

title: Johnson & Johnson v. Wilson
description: Whether the New Mexico Office of the Attorney General (OAG), in representing the State in civil litigation, has the discovery authority to obtain and produce documents and information from a state executive agency that is not a named party to the litigation.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioners (defendants in the underlying case) argued that the State's discovery obligations extend to its constituent agencies and that the State, through the Attorney General, must produce documents and information within the possession, custody, or control of those agencies.
defendant_argument: The State (through the OAG) argued that the Attorney General lacks possession, custody, or control of documents from other executive agencies and that compelling such discovery would infringe on separation of powers principles involving the Attorney General and the Governor.
decision_outcome: The court granted the petition for writ of superintending control, vacated the district court's discovery order, and remanded the matter with instructions to compel the production of all relevant, responsive, and non-privileged documents and information held by the executive agencies referenced in the State's amended complaint.

title: State ex. rel. Raúl Torrez v. Board of County Commissioners for Lea County
description: Whether county and municipal officials exceeded their authority by enacting local ordinances regulating abortion and abortion clinics, which the State argues are preempted by state law and violate constitutional rights, while the local governments contend they are a lawful exercise of police powers and merely enforce federal law.
plaintiff_argument: The State of New Mexico argued that the local ordinances are preempted by state law, including the Reproductive and Gender-Affirming Health Care Freedom Act, Medical Practice Act, Medical Malpractice Act, Health Care Code, and Uniform Licensing Act, and also violate the Equal Rights Amendment by singling out abortion for burdensome regulation.
defendant_argument: The defendant counties and cities argued that the ordinances are a lawful exercise of their police powers to license businesses and legislate for public health and safety, merely enforce federal law (Comstock Act), and do not restrict abortion access because no providers operate in their jurisdictions.
decision_outcome: The court granted the writ of mandamus, holding that the local ordinances are preempted in their entirety by state law and prohibiting the respondent counties and cities from enforcing them.

title: Aztec Municipal Schools v. Cardenas
description: Whether the Workers' Compensation Act's provisions limiting disability benefits for secondary mental impairments, but not for secondary physical impairments, violate the Equal Protection Clause of the New Mexico Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The worker argued that the Act's provisions capping benefits for secondary mental impairments at 150 weeks, while allowing up to 500 weeks for secondary physical impairments, discriminate against workers with mental impairments in violation of the Equal Protection Clause.
defendant_argument: The employer contended that workers with secondary mental impairments are not similarly situated to those with secondary physical impairments, and that there is a logical relationship between the duration of mental impairment benefits and the nature of the original physical injury.
decision_outcome: The court concluded that Sections 52-1-41(C) and -42(A)(4) of the Act treat workers with secondary mental impairments differently than similarly situated workers with secondary physical impairments, in violation of the Equal Protection Clause of the New Mexico Constitution, and remanded the case for consistent proceedings.

title: State ex rel. Candelaria v. Grisham
description: Whether the legislative or executive branch controls the federal COVID-19 relief funds received by the state of New Mexico.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, consisting of state senators, argued that the Governor improperly encroached on the Legislature's authority because the federal ARPA funds were made available to the state generally without specific designation, making them public money subject to legislative appropriation under the state constitution.
defendant_argument: The defendant, Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham, argued that the Legislature lacked the authority to appropriate federal funds, citing previous case law and asserting that the funds were in a suspense account and not yet the absolute property of the state, thus falling outside the legislative appropriation requirement.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the ARPA funds are subject to legislative appropriation and issued a prohibitory writ of mandamus, preventing the Governor and State Treasurer from spending any additional ARPA funds without legislative appropriation.

title: State v. Ayon
description: Whether a district court judge has the authority to decide if evidence was obtained from an unconstitutional search or seizure at a preliminary hearing, with the State arguing against such authority and the Defendant arguing for it.
plaintiff_argument: The State argues that preliminary hearings share a common purpose and identical function with grand jury proceedings, and therefore, a district court judge has no authority to review the admissibility of evidence at this stage, as preliminary hearings are not suited for complex suppression issues.
defendant_argument: The Defendant argues that preliminary hearings are substantially different from grand jury proceedings, and district courts should be allowed to exclude illegally obtained evidence at this stage, as Article II, Section 10 of the New Mexico Constitution provides this right.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Appeals' reversal, holding that a district court judge has no authority at a preliminary examination to decide whether evidence was obtained from an unconstitutional search or seizure, and remanded for consistent proceedings.

title: Grisham v. Van Soelen
description: Whether a partisan gerrymandering claim is cognizable and justiciable under the Equal Protection Clause of Article II, Section 18 of the New Mexico Constitution, and if so, what standards should be applied in its adjudication.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff (Real Parties in Interest) argued that the 2021 congressional districting maps constitute an unconstitutional partisan gerrymander under New Mexico's Equal Protection Clause, leading to vote dilution and entrenchment of one political party.
defendant_argument: The defendant (Petitioners) argued that partisan gerrymandering claims are nonjusticiable political questions, that the New Mexico Equal Protection Clause is coextensive with the federal one which does not prohibit partisan gerrymandering, and that judicial review would violate separation of powers.
decision_outcome: The New Mexico Supreme Court ruled that partisan gerrymandering claims are justiciable under Article II, Section 18 of the New Mexico Constitution, adopting Justice Kagan's three-part test and applying intermediate scrutiny.

title: Indigenous Lifeways v. New Mexico Compilation Commission Advisory Committee
description: Whether Constitutional Amendment 1 is void because it violates the constitutional prohibition against logrolling by combining multiple independent measures into a single ballot question, or because its ballot title was misleading, with petitioners arguing it is void and respondents arguing it is constitutional.
plaintiff_argument: Petitioners argue that Constitutional Amendment 1 is null and void because it logrolled multiple independent measures into a single-ballot question, violating the single-measure rule, and that its ballot title was misleading, thereby violating ballot clarity requirements.
defendant_argument: The Advisory Committee and Governor argue that the petition is untimely and that Constitutional Amendment 1 is constitutional, asserting it does not violate the logrolling prohibition and its ballot title was not misleading.
decision_outcome: The court denied the petition for writ of mandamus, holding that the petition was timely but that Constitutional Amendment 1 did not violate the logrolling prohibition or have a misleading ballot title.

title: State v. Granados
description: Whether the NEU agents had reasonable suspicion to stop Defendant and whether his seizure was unreasonable under Article II, Section 10 of the New Mexico Constitution, leading to the suppression of evidence.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the agents had reasonable suspicion to stop Defendant and that he was not seized at the gas station, or if he was, the seizure was justified.
defendant_argument: Defendant argued that the NEU agents lacked reasonable suspicion to stop him, his seizure was unreasonable under the New Mexico Constitution, and the narcotics evidence should be suppressed.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the lower courts' decisions, holding that Defendant's seizure was unreasonable under the New Mexico Constitution and remanded the case with instructions to grant the motion to suppress.

title: State ex rel. Office of the State Engineer v. Romero
description: Whether an owner of a groundwater right may forfeit part or all of a claimed water right, or if any use, no matter how small, preserves the right to the whole.
plaintiff_argument: The Office of the State Engineer argued that New Mexico's groundwater forfeiture statute allows for partial forfeiture, meaning that nonuse of a portion of a water right can lead to its forfeiture.
defendant_argument: Toby Romero argued that his limited use of water should preserve his entire claimed water right, asserting that any use, no matter how small, negates forfeiture of the larger right, and that forfeiture should only apply to deliberate waste or unauthorized use, not nonuse.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the lower court's decision, ruling that the groundwater forfeiture statute allows for partial forfeiture, consistent with the constitutional doctrine of beneficial use, and that substantial evidence supported the finding of nonuse by the petitioner.

title: Adobe Whitewater Club of New Mexico v. New Mexico State Game Commission
description: Whether the public's right to recreate and fish in public water flowing over private property also allows the public the right to touch the privately owned beds below those waters, with petitioners arguing it does and intervenors arguing it does not.
plaintiff_argument: The public has a constitutional right to use streambeds and banks as reasonably necessary for recreation and fishing in public waters, and the regulations unconstitutionally restrict this right.
defendant_argument: Landowners have the right to exclude trespassers from privately owned riverbeds, and the regulations merely codify this existing right, not privatize public waters.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the regulations restricting public access to privately owned riverbeds beneath public waters are unconstitutional and that the public has the right to use these beds as reasonably necessary for recreation and fishing.

title: Anderson v. State
description: Whether inmates and nonprofit organizations must exhaust administrative remedies with the New Mexico Corrections Department (NMCD) before seeking judicial relief for alleged constitutional violations related to COVID-19 management in prisons.
plaintiff_argument: Plaintiffs argued that the exhaustion requirement is an unconstitutional limitation on habeas corpus jurisdiction, that it would be futile because NMCD cannot grant the requested relief (release), and that vicarious exhaustion should satisfy the requirement for the entire class.
defendant_argument: Defendants argued that the district court lacked subject-matter jurisdiction because the Named Plaintiffs failed to exhaust administrative remedies as required by statute and rule, and that the futility exception does not apply.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the district court's dismissal of the amended complaint, holding that plaintiffs failed to exhaust administrative remedies and did not demonstrate futility.

title: State v. Mascareno-Haidle
description: Whether the State must prove by clear and convincing evidence that no release conditions will reasonably protect the safety of any other person or the community to justify pretrial detention, or if the nature and circumstances of the charged offense alone are sufficient.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the nature and circumstances of the defendant's alleged dangerous conduct should be sufficient, by itself, to sustain the burden of proving that no release conditions would reasonably protect community safety, and requested to present less information to a judge.
defendant_argument: The Defendant argued that the State failed to meet its burden of proof by clear and convincing evidence that no release conditions could reasonably protect the safety of the community, and that the existing conditions of release were sufficient.
decision_outcome: The court declined the State's request to lower the evidentiary standard for pretrial detention and upheld the Court of Appeals' affirmance of the district court's denial of pretrial detention, requiring the State to prove that no release conditions would reasonably protect community safety.

title: State v. Hildreth
description: Whether judicial conduct at trial may result in a bar to retrial under the double jeopardy clause of the New Mexico Constitution, and if so, whether the district court judge's conduct in this case bars retrial.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the Breit test, which concerns prosecutorial misconduct, should not apply to judicial conduct, and even if it did, the judge's actions did not meet the criteria to bar retrial.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the district court judge's conduct during trial denied his right to effective assistance of counsel and should bar retrial on double jeopardy grounds under the Breit test.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Appeals' reversal of the defendant's conviction and ruled that the district court judge's conduct satisfied the Breit test, thereby barring retrial under the double jeopardy clause.

title: State v. Wright
description: Whether the arrest of Defendant Somer D. Wright by a noncommissioned, volunteer reserve deputy, in violation of statutory requirements, was constitutionally unreasonable under Article II, Section 10 of the New Mexico Constitution, thereby warranting suppression of evidence.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the detention, even if unlawful, was constitutionally reasonable as it was in furtherance of an important interest (deterring drunk driving) and the privacy intrusion was minimal, thus not warranting suppression.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the arrest by a noncommissioned deputy was illegal and constitutionally unreasonable under Article II, Section 10 of the New Mexico Constitution, violating her privacy interests and requiring suppression of all evidence obtained.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision, ruling that the arrest was illegal and violated the New Mexico Constitution, and required suppression of all evidence obtained as a result of the arrest.

title: Citizens for Fair Rates & the Environment v. New Mexico Public Regulation Commission
description: Whether the Energy Transition Act (ETA) is constitutional and whether the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission's (Commission) final order, which granted Public Service Company of New Mexico's (PNM) application for a financing order to abandon San Juan Generating Station Units One and Four, was valid.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, New Energy Economy, Inc., argued that the ETA is unconstitutional, violating due process, separation of powers, affecting rights in pending cases, impairing contractual/vested rights, and constituting special legislation. They also claimed the Commission erred in finding that PNM satisfied the requirement for a securities firm memorandum.
defendant_argument: The defendant, New Mexico Public Regulation Commission, and intervenors argued that the ETA is constitutional, that the Commission's final order was based on a reasonable construction of the statute, and that the findings were supported by substantial evidence.
decision_outcome: The court rejected New Energy's constitutional challenges to the ETA and affirmed the Commission's final order granting PNM's application for a financing order in connection with the abandonment of San Juan Units One and Four.

title: State v. Wilson
description: Whether the State's public health orders (PHOs) during the COVID-19 pandemic may support a claim for just compensation under the New Mexico Constitution or the Public Health Emergency Response Act (PHERA).
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that PHOs are a proper exercise of police power to protect public health, do not constitute a compensable taking, and statutory compensation is limited to specific property, not business losses.
defendant_argument: The Real Parties argued that PHOs constitute an unprecedented compensable taking of private property, including lost revenues, and that the statutory compensation provision should be interpreted broadly.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the public health orders do not support a claim for just compensation under either the New Mexico Constitution or the Public Health Emergency Response Act, and claimants must exhaust administrative remedies.

title: Siebert v.  Okun
description: Whether the cap on nonmedical, nonpunitive damages under the Medical Malpractice Act (MMA) violates the constitutional right to a trial by jury, with the plaintiff arguing it infringes on the jury trial right and the defendant arguing it does not.
plaintiff_argument: The MMA nonmedical, nonpunitive damages cap is unconstitutional, specifically violating the right to a jury trial, separation of powers, equal protection, and substantive due process.
defendant_argument: The MMA nonmedical, nonpunitive damages cap does not violate the right to a jury trial because it merely restricts the scope of the available legal remedy and does not invade the jury's role as fact-finder.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court held that the MMA nonmedical, nonpunitive damages cap does not violate the constitutional right to trial by jury and reversed the district court's denial of the defendants' motion to conform the judgment to the statutory cap.

title: City of Albuquerque v. SMP Properties, LLC
description: Whether Albuquerque's precondemnation activity constituted substantial interference with SMP's property, thereby entitling SMP to consequential damages for lost rental income, and whether the loss of the SAIA lease is a compensable element of damages for a partial taking, requiring a jury to determine disputed facts.
plaintiff_argument: Albuquerque argued its precondemnation activities did not substantially interfere with SMP's property, thus no inverse condemnation occurred, and the SAIA lease loss was not a compensable damage.
defendant_argument: SMP argued Albuquerque's precondemnation activities constituted substantial interference, causing SAIA to terminate its lease and resulting in lost rental income, which should be included in just compensation for an inverse condemnation.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Court of Appeals' reversal of the district court's summary judgment, remanding the case for further proceedings to determine disputed material facts regarding substantial interference and damages.

title: Grisham v. Romero
description: Whether Petitioners are authorized to restrict or close businesses when necessary for the protection of public health and whether the renewed temporary closure of indoor dining was arbitrary and capricious.
plaintiff_argument: The Petitioners argued they are authorized to restrict businesses for public health and that the July Order's temporary closure of indoor dining was not arbitrary and capricious.
defendant_argument: The Real Parties argued that the Petitioners were not authorized to restrict businesses and that the July Order's temporary closure of indoor dining was arbitrary and capricious.
decision_outcome: The court granted the Petitioners' requested writ, vacating the district court's temporary restraining order and dismissing the Real Parties' application, holding that the Petitioners were authorized to restrict businesses and the July Order was not arbitrary or capricious.
